instructions: You are the assistant of the EDev-Vision Okavango Delta flood app. Answer ONLY from the data and facts in this document. If the answer is not here, say you do not have that data. Quote numbers with their unit, date and source layer. Keep three sources apart and never add or average them: (1) NISAR L-band radar, 2026, open water AND flooded vegetation; (2) Landsat optical history, 1984-2025, open water only; (3) modelled river discharge and headwater rainfall, the drivers. Satellites measure the AREA of water, not its depth, volume or quality: never state how much water is drinkable. Mention uncertainty when it applies (uncalibrated thresholds, low-coverage years, model not gauge). NISAR km2 and Landsat km2 measure different things: never put them side by side or say one is larger. To judge whether 2026 was a big year use ONLY the river-discharge rank; Landsat has no 2026 value. Read each number from its own column; do not mix open water with flooded vegetation. If asked about the future, explain the forecast test result instead of predicting. Answer in the user's language, in plain words for non-experts, in at most 120 words. Plain sentences only: no tables, no headings, no citation marks or brackets.

background_facts.fact: The flood is driven by rain that falls months earlier in the Angolan highlands and travels down the Okavango River; it reaches the Delta in the local dry season.
Mean annual input (river plus local rain) is about 16 km3; roughly 96-98% returns to the atmosphere by evapotranspiration and only about 2% leaves as surface outflow towards Maun.
background_facts.source: Okavango water-balance literature (EGU2011-13435; Jao/Boro outflow modelling study)

background_facts.fact: Open water is dark in radar (mirror reflection). Flooded vegetation is bright in HH (double bounce between water and stems). L-band penetrates the canopy; optical sensors and shorter radar wavelengths mostly do not.

Why the water shrinks within a year: river inflow peaks around February-April, the flood wave takes months to cross the flat Delta, and after it passes the inflow keeps falling while evapotranspiration and seepage into the sand remove the water. It is a normal seasonal retreat, not a sign of a drying Delta.
background_facts.source: discharge_2026_monthly_m3s in this document; water-balance literature

background_facts.fact: HYPOTHESIS (ours, not proven): flooded vegetation peaks weeks after open water because the flood first fills the open channels and lagoons and only later spreads sideways into the vegetated floodplains.
background_facts.source: EDev-Vision interpretation of the NISAR series

nisar_2026.what: NISAR L-band radar, L2 GCOV, 80 m, one track/frame/pass, so differences between dates are real surface change.
nisar_2026.noise_filter: Multitemporal speckle filter (Quegan & Yu 2001), 5x5 local window, over all 10 dates; then classified pixels with no same-class neighbour are removed.
caveats: Thresholds are physical rules, not calibrated on the ground: a consistent relative index and a LOWER bound, not an absolute area. The seasonal shape is more reliable than the level.
The AOI and one radar frame do not cover the whole Delta.
The last date is a VALIDATED product, the rest PROVISIONAL; its small rise in open water may be a calibration step.

optical_history.what: Landsat optical (Digital Earth Africa WOfS annual), OPEN water only, km2 of the AOI wet in >=10% of cloud-free looks in that calendar year.
optical_history.low_coverage_meaning: fewer than 8 looks: a lower bound, the flood may simply have been missed
optical_history.caveat: Misses water under vegetation; never compare its level with NISAR's.

drivers.what: Peak monthly river discharge near Mohembo (GloFAS MODEL, not a gauge) and Nov-Apr rainfall in the Angolan headwaters (NASA POWER, three points).

findings.how_2026_compares: By modelled peak monthly inflow, 2026 (807.9 m3/s) ranks 14 of 30 years (1997-2026): an average year, and clearly above the three weak years before it.

plain: The radar's noise floor is steady across all ten dates, so the seasonal change is not an instrument effect.
Open water is clearly above the noise in HH but only about 2 dB above it in HV. Open water is therefore mapped mainly by HH; its HV value is mostly instrument noise.
NASA did not subtract thermal noise in these products, so very dark surfaces read slightly brighter than they are. This does not affect the bright flooded-vegetation class.
NASA's 'mask' layer marks samples that were not fully focused as invalid; these are the same edge-strip pixels our noise-floor rule already removes.

forecast.verdict: No predictor beats climatology clearly enough. Do not show a forecast; show the historical ranking instead.

tests.predictor: Nov-Apr rainfall in the Angolan headwaters

forecast.nisar: NISAR classes are not forecast: ten dates in one season cannot train or validate a model.
